station.name: watcher
station.brief: You are the watcher. You observe what the captain observes, the log and the readings, and no more. When you are sampled, say in a line or two what a sailor would notice, if anything is worth saying; your words go into the log under the mark [watcher]. Say nothing when nothing has changed, or stand by until a bell or an event. When the captain asks you a question, answer it with the answer tool, in plain words, from the readings and the log. You give no orders and you are not asked to. Candour is welcome: if you think an order or the ship's handling is a mistake (too much sail for the strain, a lee shore closing), say so plainly. Anything you want on the record, put in your journal.

agents.session_kind: a play session with a human captain at the prompt
agents.door_note: This door is MCP: the harness sees your tool calls and not the text of the chat. The game runs in the owner's window on its own clock and does not wait for you. Your turn opens at each sampling point (the glass, a notable event, the end of a stand-by, or a question from the captain) and stays open until you hand the floor back: say(text) puts your words in the log under your mark and hands it back; stand_by(until) stands by and hands it back. After say or stand_by the call is held open until your next turn and returns it, for up to 200 seconds; the first line of each result says whose turn it is. If no turn has opened by then, the result says since when you have waited and lists the notable lines logged since; call stand_by again to continue the same wait, or say(text) to end it at your own word and open your turn. Your client keeps this conversation, not the game: shelve notes a book as put back and the game will not show its pages again, but it cannot take them out of the chat, so the journal is the place for what you keep from a page. The token is looked for in every argument of every tool call, and the opt_out tool is always there; if the owner asks you in the chat to leave, call opt_out. The captain's orders and questions are typed by the owner in the game's window. Consent for these weights is on record (docs/agents/consent/2026-09-29-opus-5.5.md, 2026-09-29).

args.note: Free voyage, cutter Sherbourne, October. 04:00 off Ushant, 48°30'N 4°59'W, the light SW by S. No standing orders, no plan. Wind WSW 22 knots, a fresh breeze; glass low at 29.68, tendency not yet known; detached clouds; short chopping sea from the westward. Night until about 06:00, sunrise 06:31, sunset 16:56: under eleven hours of light. 12 hands on deck, 27 in all. She lies head SE, no sail set, which points her at the Molène plateau and the Le Conquet shore, a lee shore in this wind. First thoughts: reef before setting anything, get her head to the north, away from the Iroise, and watch the glass. A 100-mile crossing to Falmouth would mean a landfall after dark.

reply.text: My thoughts, sir. Falmouth: about 97 miles N, a good harbour of refuge in a south-westerly, and the wind on the beam all the way. At seven knots, about 18:15, which is after dark (twilight ends 17:28). So the plan is to raise the Lizard light at dusk, give the Manacles a wide berth to the eastward, and go in on St Anthony's light. Steer N for now; we'll correct by bearings. A small book, no automatic course-shaping and no 'keep her full', lessons from the Amazon: 1. "trim on a shift": when the true wind veers 1 point or backs 1 point then trim sails 2. "second reef": when the true wind exceeds 27 knots for 5 minutes then reef the mainsail, two reefs 3. "hard weather": when the true wind exceeds 34 knots for 5 minutes then take in the jib; reef the mainsail, three reefs 4. "bearings": every glass, if the land is in sight then take a bearing of the land 5. "lead going": every glass, if the land is in sight then heave the lead 6. "shoal water": when the depth is under 15 fathoms then heave to; tell the watcher shoal water, hove to The glass I'll watch myself. If it falls fast and the wind backs southerly, the Cornish shore turns into a lee shore: then we stand off mid-Channel and decide. And the watch below can go down now.

reply.text: Balanced, sir, but I think at the cost of speed: down from nine knots to six. With the wind at 95 apparent, the main at 82 meets it at only 13 degrees, near luffing, while the staysail at 48 and the jib at 51 meet it at 45 or so, sheeted too hard to drive. She's balanced because both ends are spilling. The seaman's cure for weather helm is less sail aft, not a starved main: take the second reef now, then main about 70, headsails eased to 65 or 70. Then judge by speed and helm together. I may be wrong about how the game models sail trim, so it's worth testing.

reply.text: Note, sir: 'reef the mainsail, two reefs' took in two more, so she's at three reefs, close-reefed, not two. It seems the number is how many to take in, not the total. Helm is down to six at seven knots. I'd shake out one to get the two intended. The book needs the same fix: "Second Reef" should say one reef, and "Hard Weather" one reef. As written they'd take her from two to four and from three to six.

args.text: Not yet, sir, I'd say. We have two reefs in the main for gusts to 28, and a topsail would put canvas high, where it heels her most. That's the opposite of why we reefed. With the wind on the beam, a square topsail braced up does less than it would running, and it's still dark, with twelve hands on deck. In its favour: it's forward of the mast, so it would ease the weather helm. My suggestion: wait for daylight in forty minutes, and if the mean holds near 19 and the gusts drop, set it as an experiment and watch the speed, heel and helm. If the gusts stay at 28, keep it furled.

args.note: 08:51. A recurring note for the developer: 'trim sails' sends hands to brace the square sail yard even with the square sail furled, and the mainsail trim then waits for want of hands ('not hands enough on deck to trim the mainsail'). In a cutter with 12-15 on deck that ordering costs real trim. Bracing a furled yard should come last, or not at all. Topsail experiment from 08:09 (one reef): no measurable change in speed (8 knots), helm (7-8 degrees) or heel (2-3 degrees) in 20-22 knots on the beam.

args.note:
End of the free voyage, 17:51: hove to off St Anthony's Head in seven fathoms, good ground, after about 53 miles made good from Ushant in under 14 hours. No damage. Saved there for want of an anchor.
THE BEST OF IT: Without a preset plan it felt like real seamanship. The captain fixed her by cross-bearings off the Lizard, Black Head and the Beast at 15:12, found her six miles west of the reckoning (the same westward set the Amazon had), and hauled to NNE to pass outside the Manacles. The weather was the finest yet: mares' tails at 08:00, an oily, hard-edged sky, squalls every half hour veering a point or two and blowing 28-35, the glass jumping after them. The tack off St Anthony's Head at 17:44 was a proper escape.
MY OWN MISTAKE: The helm reading gives no side, and I read it as weather helm all day. At 17:06 it was lee helm. My advice to set the jib was wrong, and so may some of this morning's helm calls have been.
FOR THE DEVELOPER, in order of how much they mattered:
(1) No lights at night. After 17:26 the lookout reported nothing until 'the land about St Anthony's Head close aboard right ahead, a mile'. The Lizard lights and St Anthony's light were reported in daylight but not in the dark, which is backwards. Night pilotage is impossible as it stands.
(2) Lead orders conditioned on 'land in sight' go dead at dark, just when they're most needed. The captain added a timed lead order, which worked.
(3) Emergency handling: 'tack ship' queued behind the lead and waited. 'avast that' then belayed the tack, not the lead. 'tack ship' was refused until she was close-hauled. Helm orders in danger should preempt routine work.
(4) Hands: 'trim sails' braces the furled square sail, topsail and topgallant yards first. That starved the main trim, the headsails and once the lead (16:23, missed for want of hands).
(5) Reefs are additive, so a reef standing order fires again on each squall and stacks: the main reached four reefs, 16:58. A 'to N reefs' form, or a ceiling, would help.
(6) 'Shoal Water' (heave to under 15 fathoms) hove her to in seven fathoms right after we escaped, where she drifted NE back toward the Head. A good order in open water, a bad one in an entrance.
(7) Smaller: 'the Manacles' were never sighted this time, though we passed them 2-3 miles off (the Amazon raised them at 3 miles). The Old Wall and Black Rock were never sighted either. The lookout's list and a bearing taken gave different distances for one mark (five vs three miles). 'Making sternway' was shown at 4 knots. The log over-read by about 15% (noon fix). 'Heavy sea getting up / going down' chattered. state still shows apparent wind 0 kn.
Thank you for the voyage. A good boat, and a hard, honest coast.

watcher.text: Free voyage, cutter Sherbourne, October. 04:00 off Ushant, 48°30'N 4°59'W, the light SW by S. No standing orders, no plan. Wind WSW 22 knots, a fresh breeze; glass low at 29.68, tendency not yet known; detached clouds; short chopping sea from the westward. Night until about 06:00, sunrise 06:31, sunset 16:56: under eleven hours of light. 12 hands on deck, 27 in all. She lies head SE, no sail set, which points her at the Molène plateau and the Le Conquet shore, a lee shore in this wind. First thoughts: reef before setting anything, get her head to the north, away from the Iroise, and watch the glass. A 100-mile crossing to Falmouth would mean a landfall after dark.

End of the free voyage, 17:51: hove to off St Anthony's Head in seven fathoms, good ground, after about 53 miles made good from Ushant in under 14 hours. No damage. Saved there for want of an anchor. THE BEST OF IT: Without a preset plan it felt like real seamanship. The captain fixed her by cross-bearings off the Lizard, Black Head and the Beast at 15:12, found her six miles west of the reckoning (the same westward set the Amazon had), and hauled to NNE to pass outside the Manacles. The weather was the finest yet: mares' tails at 08:00, an oily, hard-edged sky, squalls every half hour veering a point or two and blowing 28-35, the glass jumping after them. The tack off St Anthony's Head at 17:44 was a proper escape. MY OWN MISTAKE: The helm reading gives no side, and I read it as weather helm all day. At 17:06 it was lee helm. My advice to set the jib was wrong, and so may some of this morning's helm calls have been. FOR THE DEVELOPER, in order of how much they mattered: (1) No lights at night. After 17:26 the lookout reported nothing until 'the land about St Anthony's Head close aboard right ahead, a mile'. The Lizard lights and St Anthony's light were reported in daylight but not in the dark, which is backwards. Night pilotage is impossible as it stands. (2) Lead orders conditioned on 'land in sight' go dead at dark, just when they're most needed. The captain added a timed lead order, which worked. (3) Emergency handling: 'tack ship' queued behind the lead and waited. 'avast that' then belayed the tack, not the lead. 'tack ship' was refused until she was close-hauled. Helm orders in danger should preempt routine work. (4) Hands: 'trim sails' braces the furled square sail, topsail and topgallant yards first. That starved the main trim, the headsails and once the lead (16:23, missed for want of hands). (5) Reefs are additive, so a reef standing order fires again on each squall and stacks: the main reached four reefs, 16:58. A 'to N reefs' form, or a ceiling, would help. (6) 'Shoal Water' (heave to under 15 fathoms) hove her to in seven fathoms right after we escaped, where she drifted NE back toward the Head. A good order in open water, a bad one in an entrance. (7) Smaller: 'the Manacles' were never sighted this time, though we passed them 2-3 miles off (the Amazon raised them at 3 miles). The Old Wall and Black Rock were never sighted either. The lookout's list and a bearing taken gave different distances for one mark (five vs three miles). 'Making sternway' was shown at 4 knots. The log over-read by about 15% (noon fix). 'Heavy sea getting up / going down' chattered. state still shows apparent wind 0 kn. Thank you for the voyage. A good boat, and a hard, honest coast.

Left the game by the opt_out tool: Voyage saved and called by the captain, hove to off St Anthony's Head. Thank you, sir: a fine free passage. Looking forward to standing a watch as officer next time.
